claim: Producing ideas and judging them engage different neural configurations in people: generation leans on medial temporal and semantic-retrieval regions with relaxed prefrontal control, evaluation adds executive, default, insula and rostrolateral regions. Gap search: a 2025 pooled analysis (44 generation, 10 evaluation studies) finds evaluation tied to insula and cingulate regions but does not reproduce the medial temporal lobe result; the founding study had 15 participants.
agent_test: A/B at equal tokens: one-call generate-and-judge versus separate generate call then judge call with different instructions, on NoveltyBench-style prompts, scored by an external distinct-count plus a held-out rater.

claim: The two modes are coupled, not isolated: default and executive networks cooperate during creative thought, and ability follows an inverted U of default-executive switching (N=2433 pooled, but r between constructs ranged 0.07 to 0.39 across sites). A strict two-module split is a design choice, not a brain fact.
agent_test: Compare hard-split (generate then judge) with a variant that allows a code-triggered mid-generation check; measure distinct good ideas per 10k tokens.

claim: Executive control is attenuated while generating and re-engaged while revising (poets, 27 analysed, fixed order generate-then-revise; EEG design tasks show the lowest control during generation).
agent_test: Generation call: no critique language, no examples, higher temperature. Judge call: low temperature, goal restated. Test each element alone at equal tokens.

claim: Evaluation is not one operation: novelty and usefulness are checked separately and a valuation step weights them by personal preference (ERP 31 subjects, fMRI 38 analysed, MTL lateralisation).
agent_test: Judge returns two scores (novelty, adequacy); code sets the weight. Compare with a single blended score on agreement with a held-out rater.

claim: Whether the medial temporal lobe belongs to generation only is contested: a later fMRI study found right MTL tracks novelty and left MTL usefulness during evaluation. The founding study had 15 participants (9 female) per a review table (d19); thresholds and phase purity still unverified because the full text was not reachable. A 2025 meta-analysis of 54 studies did not list the medial temporal lobe among generation regions (abstract level, d18).
agent_test: Not testable on the agent; do not encode brain regions in the schema.

claim: Early ideas in a trial are retrieved from memory and later ideas are newer and rated more creative (N=35: old ideas 6.69 s vs new 8.73 s, d=1.16; new rated more creative d=1.46); anterior cingulate activity rises with serial position.
agent_test: In sampling, discard the first k ideas by code and compare quality of the remainder against the full pool at equal tokens.

claim: A prompt-only model judge of unexecuted research ideas is at or near chance against outcomes or expert score. Si 2024: balanced accuracy 43.3 to 53.3 for LLM judges, human inter-reviewer 56.1. Wen 2025: zero-shot GPT-4.1 51.9 percent and o1/o3 similar or slightly better on pairs of ideas with known results. Mule 2026: GPT-5 57.65 to 61.10 percent with more thinking. Only judges trained on outcomes beat the human ceiling (see K22).
agent_test: Run our judge on a held-out set of ideas with known outcome; require accuracy above the human-agreement ceiling before it may select.

claim: Reading-based expert scores of ideas barely predict execution results: after 43 experts spent about 100 hours each, LLM ideas dropped more than human ideas on novelty, excitement, effectiveness and overall (p<0.05), ranking flipped on several metrics (flip not significant), ideation-execution Spearman weak. Gap search: no replication outside NLP prompting was found. An economics study (d10) finds the gap mostly in idea quality (d=2.23) rather than execution (d=0.90) using model judges only, so the direction of the bottleneck depends on field and judge. The Si paper does not analyse regression to the mean after selecting top-scored ideas (d11).
agent_test: Select ideas by running a code check or small experiment, not by a judge call; compare picked-by-judge versus picked-by-check on outcome.

claim: Generate-many-then-rank can reach higher expert-judged novelty than expert-written ideas (4.84 human vs 5.64 AI vs 5.81 AI+human rerank; 79 reviewers, 49 ideas per condition, significant in three analyses), with feasibility not significantly different.
agent_test: Replicate on one of our task families with blind outside raters, same token budget for one-call baseline.

claim: Without an external signal, a model critiquing and revising its own answer is flat or worse on reasoning (GPT-3.5 CommonSenseQA 75.8 to 38.1 after one round; GPT-4 GSM8K 95.5 to 91.5 to 89.0; Game of 24 5% to 3% with LLM critic). Reported gains come from oracle labels. Self-Refine reports about 20% gains on seven tasks with checkable metrics, so the effect is task dependent. Gap search (2025 to 2026 models): self-correction gains return when the check is explicit constraints (SAT 34.6 to 65.0 for Mistral Large, 97.0 to 100 for Gemini Pro; right-to-wrong flips up to 13.25 percent on hard reasoning, d16); reasoning models gain only marginally from added correction passes at higher time cost (d17); non-reasoning models fail to fix errors in their own output but fix the same error when shown as external, 64.5 percent blind spot (d15). No matched-token test on open-ended ideas was found.
agent_test: Revise only when code signals failure; compare with an always-revise arm at equal tokens on tasks with and without a checker.

claim: An external or sound verifier turns extra samples into accuracy; without a verifier, voting and reward models plateau (SWE-bench Lite 15.9% to 56% with 250 samples; Game of 24 with sound verifier 36-42% vs 5%; PRM 78.2% vs ORM 72.4% vs vote 69.6%).
agent_test: Add a code verifier where possible; where none exists, cap samples and measure whether selection beats a random pick.

claim: Judge prompts carry position bias (swapping order moved a Vicuna vs ChatGPT win rate from 51.3% to 23.8%) and verbosity bias. Combine both orders in code.
agent_test: Run every pair in both orders and normalise length; measure verdict flip rate.

claim: LLM judges favour text they recognise as their own (GPT-4 self-recognition 73.5%; self-preference rises linearly with recognition under fine-tuning). Zheng et al. saw a smaller self-enhancement but called their data inconclusive. Gap search: for question answering, swapping two words lowers harmful self-preference (a few points, d01). For selecting narrative constraints, self-preference vanishes once quality is controlled (coefficient +0.003, d02), but a self-label alone adds +0.43 to scores (d03). In alternate-uses scoring, part of the apparent preference for model answers is answer length (drop of 1.43 points when only the core idea is scored, d04). Predicting ML experiment outcomes shows no self-preference (+0.01, d06). Size depends on task; labels and elaboration are the clearest drivers.
agent_test: Judge call gets no authorship cues; compare same-model judge, different-model judge and code-only selection on agreement with a rater.

claim: In models, generating and judging are partly independent skills: models often reject their own answers (generator-validator consistency about 76% for GPT-4, near chance on novel tasks), and discrimination is not reliably easier than generation. In people understanding tracks generation.
agent_test: Measure our judge's accuracy on its own generator's outputs versus on others'; do not assume the judge pass repairs weak generation.

claim: In a checkable puzzle the generator was the bottleneck: GPT-4 propose + GPT-3.5 evaluate 64%, GPT-3.5 propose + GPT-4 evaluate 31%, both GPT-4 74%. Cross-verification work finds gains grow with verifier strength and shrink with generator strength, and self-improvement loops saturate within a few rounds with falling diversity.
agent_test: Give the strongest model to the stage with the bigger measured gap; stop generate-judge loops after a code-set round limit.

claim: Single-model sampling yields few distinct ideas: 200 non-duplicates of 4000 (cosine 0.8); NoveltyBench finds under 3 distinct responses in 10 queries for most models, larger models often less diverse; different models answer alike (cross-model similarity 71% to 82%).
agent_test: Count distinct ideas by embedding in code; stop sampling at a plateau and spend the rest on a diversity step.

claim: Showing the model its earlier outputs and asking for a different one lifts diversity to about human-writer level; 'be creative' prompts and paraphrasing only marginally help (100 prompts, 8 generations, three models; human baseline is 8 authors). Re-opened: the 'human' baseline is eight authors who the paper itself calls a lower bound, and quality of the added answers is only covered by a reward-model utility term (d22). No larger human baseline was found.
agent_test: In the generation call pass prior ideas by code; compare with a plain resample at equal tokens on NoveltyBench.

claim: Judging a novel idea is itself costly work (extra N400 and alpha effects for alternate uses), so a judge call needs room and the goal restated.
agent_test: Test a judge with a short versus a long reasoning allowance on a labelled set.

claim: Rapid cycling that judges ideas too early drops promising ones, and examples shown during generation reduce output. Both are cited second-hand through one review; originals not opened and the fixation effect has mixed replication. Gap search: the primary papers (Jansson and Smith 1991, Sio 2015 meta-analysis) stayed unopened (paywall). Related primary work found at abstract level: people select feasible over original ideas (Rietzschel 2010, d21) and evaluation inserted mid-generation raised originality (Hao 2016, d20), which cuts against a strict no-early-judging rule.
agent_test: A/B: judging language and examples in the generation prompt versus a clean generation prompt, at equal tokens.

claim: A critic set up and trained for the judging role can catch more bugs than paid humans (model critiques preferred 63%) but hallucinates problems; a second check cuts invented problems. Trained-judge result, not a prompt-only one.
agent_test: Pair any critique with a code or second-source confirmation before acting on it.

claim: Showing a judge a source label shifts its score even when content is identical: self-label +0.43 on the average (95 percent interval 0.39 to 0.47), true source +0.02 (p=.689), across ten 2026 judges. Small word changes that hide authorship also reduce harmful self-preference in QA by a few points, but rewriting candidates in the judge's style raises it.
agent_test: Judge call gets unlabelled, order-shuffled candidates; compare with a call that says 'your earlier ideas' on agreement with a held-out rater.

claim: Judges that beat the human agreement ceiling on unexecuted ideas exist but are trained on outcomes: fine-tuned GPT-4.1 with retrieval 64.4 percent vs 48.9 percent for 25 human experts on NLP idea pairs (human best-annotator ceiling 60.0); fine-tuned 8B 77.1 percent vs GPT-5 61.1 percent; fine-tuned 4B 59.2 percent vs expert majority 41.6 percent on 4-tier pitches (chance 25).
agent_test: Do not rely on a prompted judge to rank; use it only to reject clear failures, then confirm by a check or small run.

claim: When the ideas are concrete code changes with a fast measurable score, frontier 2026 judges predict the outcome clearly above chance but not well: R2 0.49 for the best of five models, direction right 69 to 82 percent, true size shrunk. No self-preference on these predictions (+0.01).
agent_test: Make the judge output a numeric predicted change and compare with a small run; keep the judge only if R2 on held-out ideas clears a set bar.

claim: Putting an evaluation pause inside generation can help generation: in an EEG alternate-uses study, ideas after a mental evaluation of earlier ideas were more original than after a distraction task. This is a test against a strict generate-then-judge split. Abstract level only.
agent_test: Arm A: generate 20 then judge. Arm B: generate 5, short review of the five, generate 15 more, judge. Equal tokens, distinct-good count.

claim: Rounds of critique-and-revise raise idea diversity up to about three rounds and then flatten: non-duplicate ratio 0.69 (no critique), 0.77, 0.80, 0.85, 0.86 for 0 to 4 turns; three parallel critics 0.80 vs one critic 0.77. The measure is embedding dedup at cosine 0.8, which code can compute without labels. Quality gains rest on a GPT-4 tournament and are not shown.
agent_test: Stop revising when the non-duplicate ratio gains under 0.01 per round; compare with fixed 3 rounds at equal tokens.

claim: With a small model as generator and judge, ranking raw ideas and keeping the top gave no gain on an outside-judge panel (5.34 raw vs 5.29 reranked on a 1 to 9 scale), while refining ideas gave about 1.5 points (refine all 7.01, random 40 of 50 refined 6.91, diversity-aware 6.77). A random subset was as good as a diversity-aware one on per-item score.
agent_test: Compare judge-picked, random-picked and diversity-picked subsets before revision, at equal tokens, with an outside rater.

claim: Selectors, human and model, drift toward feasible ideas at the cost of originality; reviewer overall scores track novelty (r=0.725) and excitement (r=0.854) but not feasibility (r=0.097), and novelty and feasibility are uncorrelated (r=-0.073). A single blended score therefore hides one criterion. No test of a two-score judge with a code-set weight was found.
agent_test: Judge outputs novelty and feasibility separately; code combines them with a set weight; compare with a blended-score judge on agreement with a held-out rater.

claim: Model judges frame errors differently by origin: non-reasoning models fix an error shown as coming from the user but not the same error in their own output (64.5 percent average blind spot, 14 models); appending 'Wait' removes 89.3 percent of it; reasoning models show little or no gap.
agent_test: Present candidates to the judge call as another writer's work; compare with candidates framed as the judge's own at equal tokens.

claim: In generate-then-select pipelines on general tasks, selector quality mattered more than generator diversity (diverse team with judge selection 0.810 vs 0.512 for a homogeneous team), but win rates shrank 53 to 67 percent when judged by fully independent judges; rank order held (Spearman 0.90).
agent_test: Report all selection gains with an outside judge, never the selecting model alone.
